system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2158-11-15 20:41:00 to 2158-11-18 13:36:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old woman with a history of chronic myeloid leukemia s/p stem cell transplant, chronic GVHD, diabetes, and prior DVT/PE was admitted for a non-healing left leg ulcer and antibiotic-associated diarrhea. She had sustained a leg injury 22 days prior, and despite oral antibiotics, the wound failed to heal. Diarrhea developed on doxycycline but resolved after discontinuation. On admission, she was started on vancomycin, but it was discontinued on hospital day 2 due to lack of infection signs and negative wound culture. A bedside debridement was performed to remove necrotic tissue impeding healing. IVIG was given for low IgG levels. Her pain was managed with oral hydromorphone, and she was discharged home with wound care instructions, a short course of pain medication, and follow-up planned. Weight loss was attributed to recent poor intake from gastrointestinal symptoms.
problems: Non-pressure chronic ulcer of other part of left lower leg with unspecified severity
Adverse effect of tetracyclines, initial encounter
Type 2 diabetes mellitus with other skin ulcer
Personal history of other venous thrombosis and embolism

Dear Ms. ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you. You were recently admitted 
to ___ after a fall. You were found 
to have a fracture of your sternum (breast bone) and left rib 
fractures. Please follow the below instructions to continue your 
recovery. 

* Your injury caused left 6th rib fracture which can cause 
severe pain and subsequently cause you to take shallow breaths 
because of the pain.
 
* You should take your pain medication as directed to stay ahead 
of the pain otherwise you won't be able to take deep breaths. If 
the pain medication is too sedating take half the dose and 
notify your physician.
 
* Pneumonia is a complication of rib fractures.  In order to 
decrease your risk you must use your incentive spirometer 4 
times every hour while awake.  This will help expand the small 
airways in your lungs and assist in coughing up secretions that 
pool in the lungs.
 
* You will be more comfortable if you use a cough pillow to hold 
against your chest and guard your rib cage while coughing and 
deep breathing.
 
* Symptomatic relief with ice packs or heating pads for short 
periods may ease the pain.
 
* Narcotic pain medication can cause constipation therefore you 
should take a stool softener twice daily and increase your fluid 
and fiber intake if possible.
 
* Do NOT smoke
 
* If your doctor allows, non-steroidal ___ drugs 
are very effective in controlling pain ( ie, Ibuprofen, Motrin, 
Advil, Aleve, Naprosyn) but they have their own set of side 
effects so make sure your doctor approves.

shortness of breath, increased pain or crackling sensation 
around your ribs (crepitus).

pool in the lungs.

deep breathing.

periods may ease the pain.

should take a stool softener twice daily and increase your fluid 
and fiber intake if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I was in a car accident three days ago. I was a passenger, wearing a seatbelt, and I walked away at the scene. But my chest pain has been getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You came to the ED today because the pain didn’t improve. Any shortness of breath, dizziness, or numbness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’m breathing okay. Just sharp pain when I move or cough. It’s right in the center of my chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your imaging. A CT scan shows a fracture in your sternum — that’s the breastbone in the center of your chest. There’s also a new fracture in your left 6th rib.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is it serious? Could it affect my heart or lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The good news is, there’s no damage to your heart, lungs, or major blood vessels. No bleeding in the chest. The fracture is stable, so surgery isn’t needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. I was worried after the last hospital stay. I’ve had so many health issues since my stem cell transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see you have chronic graft-versus-host disease and a history of blood clots. That’s why we’re keeping you on your blood thinner, enoxaparin, to prevent any new clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I’ve been on that for a while. Should I be concerned about bleeding with the fracture?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring your labs closely. Your blood counts are stable, and there’s no sign of internal bleeding. The benefits of staying on the blood thinner outweigh the risks right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about the pain? It’s hard to take deep breaths.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on oxycodone and acetaminophen for pain, plus a lidocaine patch over the area. We’ll also give you an incentive spirometer to help you breathe deeply and avoid pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. I’ll use it every hour when I’m awake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We also did a head CT to be safe — no brain injury or skull fracture. And your pelvis and spine scans show no new fractures, just old compression changes you already had.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my spine has been fragile for years. I’m just glad nothing else is broken.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little better. The patch helps, but the oxycodone makes me sleepy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to Dilaudid, which is another pain medication that might control the pain better with less drowsiness. We’ll start with a low dose and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it. Any other tests today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a stool test yesterday to rule out C. diff, since you’ve had GI issues before. It came back negative, so no infection. Your liver enzymes are a bit high, but that’s likely from your GVHD, not new trauma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my liver has been acting up. My specialist is managing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another chest X-ray today because you mentioned right-sided pain. It shows no new fractures or lung issues. The sternal fracture is still there, but healing will take time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the right side pain is probably just muscle strain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely. Trauma can cause widespread soreness. We’ll keep managing your pain and encourage you to keep moving gently to avoid stiffness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning look stable. Hemoglobin is a bit lower, but not dropping. Pain seems better with the Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. I’m able to sit up and walk to the bathroom without too much trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. You’re also breathing well and using the spirometer. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if everything stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What will I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue the enoxaparin for blood thinning. For pain, you’ll have acetaminophen, ibuprofen for mild pain, and Dilaudid as needed for moderate pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ibuprofen is okay? I thought it might affect my stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on omeprazole, which protects your stomach, so short-term ibuprofen should be safe. But take it with food and stop if you feel any discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the lidocaine patch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, use one patch daily over the painful area. Also, keep using the incentive spirometer 4 times an hour while awake to prevent pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Should I avoid driving or lifting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No heavy lifting for at least 6 weeks. Driving is okay once you’re off narcotics. Since you’re on Dilaudid now, wait until your pain is controlled with milder meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Any follow-up appointments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your primary doctor will see you in a week. If you have increasing pain, trouble breathing, or a fever, go to the ER right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well — pain controlled, eating, walking. We’re ready to discharge you home with services for a few days to help with daily tasks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take pain meds on schedule, use the spirometer, and don’t push yourself. Healing takes time, especially with your medical history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it slow. Thanks for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. A nurse will go over your discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in before you go. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Use the spirometer, watch for breathing problems, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ve done a great job following the plan. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Get some rest and keep healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old woman with a history of chronic graft-versus-host disease, prior stem cell transplant, and history of venous thromboembolism was admitted after worsening chest pain following a motor vehicle accident three days prior. Imaging revealed an acute sternal fracture and an acute left 6th rib fracture, with no evidence of intrathoracic injury. She was admitted for pain control and monitoring. Pain was initially managed with oxycodone and a lidocaine patch, then transitioned to hydromorphone (Dilaudid) for better control. She remained hemodynamically stable, afebrile, and was able to ambulate and tolerate oral intake. Incentive spirometry was used to prevent pulmonary complications. She was discharged home with services on hospital day 3 with a pain regimen including acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and PRN hydromorphone, along with continued enoxaparin for thromboprophylaxis. Follow-up was arranged with her primary care provider.
